They differ, however, on his wealth: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr put it at a thousand dinars, Qatada at four or six thousand, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab took it to be a month's income after month, al-Nu'man ibn Salim a piece of land, and Muqatil a garden at al-Ta'if that never ceased to bear fruit. On the number of his sons, Mujahid and Qatada count ten, Sa'id ibn Jubayr thirteen, and Muqatil seven. All agree that the sa'ud is a climb of fire in Hell, though some describe a smooth rock and others an unending hardship. The reports say al-Walid reflected on the Qur'an, then called it magic handed down or human speech, for which he is cursed. The keepers of Hell are nineteen; al-Mawardi explains the number by a logic of arithmetic, while Ibn Kathir relies on prophetic reports to confirm it.

The commentators read this verse as part of God's threat against al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi. God tells His Prophet to leave him to the One who created him alone, without wealth or children. God then gave him abundant, far-reaching wealth, sons who were always present with him, and ease in life and status. He hoped for more, but God denies it because of his stubborn rejection of the Qur'an's verses. Almost all agree that the 'extended wealth' (mal mamdud) means great riches that keep growing through income from crops, livestock and trade. They differ on the amount. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say a thousand dinars, Qatada six thousand, Sufyan four thousand, one report from Mujahid gives a hundred thousand, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab says it was a month's yield each month. Al-Nu'man ibn Salim takes it to be land. Al-Tabari concludes that one should keep to the general sense of great wealth, while al-Razi finds the precise figures arbitrary. Al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the term may cover several sources of gain. For the sons who were 'present', Mujahid and Qatada count ten, Sa'id ibn Jubayr thirteen, and al-Suddi twelve, while Ibn 'Abbas explains that they are present in the sense of being mentioned alongside him. The context is a warning that ingratitude brings the loss of blessings.

This verse describes the sons who stood beside their father as witnesses, always present with him and never absent. The commentators differ on their number: Mujahid and Qatada say ten, Ibn Jubayr says thirteen, and Muqatil names seven, three of whom later embraced Islam. The most common reading of shuhudan is that they were constantly present, either because he needed them or because he feared being apart from them, while others take it to mean that they attended assemblies and their testimony was heard, or that they were mentioned alongside their father, as Ibn Abbas held. The verse belongs to a passage about the blessings given to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, followed by his denial of those blessings and his hostility to the Quran. The exegetes agree that the passage concerns him: it recounts his wealth, his children and his standing, and notes that he still hoped for more, which God rejected with a firm refusal and a threat. Several reports say that after the revelation his wealth and children declined until he died, though the sources present this as a narration rather than a general principle. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi transmit these views without deciding between them.

The commentators explain that this passage concerns al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, and that God reminds him of the favours he received: he was created alone, without wealth or children, then given abundant property and sons who remained always present with him, and God spread out his life for him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand this as widening and easing his means of livelihood; Mujahid connects it to wealth piled layer upon layer like a bedding, Ibn 'Abbas to the broad lands he held between Yemen and Syria, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi read it as lofty status and leadership, al-Walid being called "the solitary" and "the fragrant herb of Quraysh." Because he then hoped for still more, God rebuffed him with "No." The scholars differ on what he hoped for: al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it as more wealth and children in this world, while al-Hasan takes it as entry into Paradise, since al-Walid is said to have claimed that Paradise was made only for him if Muhammad was truthful. Al-Baghawi and al-Razi report that his prosperity declined after the revelation until he died. The reason given for the refusal is his stubborn opposition to God's signs, which al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy connect with the Qur'an itself. The commentators agree that the lesson is that favour received should not breed arrogance or obstinate rejection.

These verses concern al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. God tells His Prophet to leave him, the one He created alone, without wealth or children, and then gave him abundant property, sons who stayed beside him, and an easy life. Yet he hopes for more, and the word "Nay" that follows rejects that hope. The commentators agree that the verses were revealed about him and that he was refused more because he opposed God's signs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that he had ten sons, Ibn Jubayr counts thirteen, and Muqatil counts seven. The wealth is estimated differently: a thousand dinars according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, more according to others, and a monthly income according to Umar. Most explain "sa'ud" as a painful torment. Ibn Kathir, citing al-Tabari, also transmits the hadith of Abu Said about a mountain of fire in Hell, but notes that its chain contains irregularities. The commentators then recount the story of al-Walid's reflection on the Qur'an, which led him to call it magic or human speech. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir narrate it with variations in the details. All agree that the verses express a severe warning to whoever rejects the truth after recognising it.

These verses, as the commentators explain them, concern al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, who had been given wealth, sons and status yet wanted still more. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid put his wealth at a thousand dinars or more, while others speak of an orchard or a monthly income; his sons, always present with him, are counted as ten by some and thirteen by others. The word 'kalla' that follows is a rebuke that cuts off his hope, and God gives the reason: he was stubbornly opposed to His signs after knowing them. Scholars differ on 'sa'ud'. Qatada and al-Hasan take it as a painful torment without relief, al-Suddi as a smooth rock in the Fire that he is forced to climb, and a report from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri describes a mountain of fire climbed for seventy autumns before one falls back. Several accounts say al-Walid reflected on the Qur'an and settled on what he would say, calling it sorcery handed down and mere human speech, and for this he was cursed. Mujahid reads 'wahidan' as created alone, without wealth or child, while others take it to mean a man whose father was unknown. On 'ʿanid', Mujahid and Abu 'Ubayda say stubborn opponent, Abu Salih one who keeps away, Qatada one who denies, and Muqatil one who turns away. On 'lawwaha lil-bashar', Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas describe a fire that burns and blackens the skin, while al-Hasan describes Hell appearing before people. Most count nineteen guardians, and the commentators debate whether this number means nineteen ranks, groups or chiefs.

These verses describe al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, whom God created alone, without wealth or children, and then provided with great wealth, sons present beside him and an easy life. He still hoped for more, but God rejects this hope and states that he was hostile to His signs. The punishment promised is a relentless hardship with no relief. Commentators explain that the word sa'ud means a steep, difficult climb, and several report, as al-Tirmidhi and Ahmad do through Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that it is a mountain of fire he is forced to climb endlessly. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir emphasise the sense of torment without rest, while others take it as an image of suffering. All agree the verses were revealed about al-Walid, but they differ on the details of his property: Ibn Abbas says a thousand dinars, Mujahid a hundred thousand, Umar a monthly income, and others a garden or lands. The number of his sons is given as seven, ten or thirteen depending on the source. Al-Walid, they report, reflected on what to say about the Qur'an, then frowned and turned away before declaring it to be sorcery or human speech, which brought him the curse. As for the nineteen guardians of the Fire, some take them to be angels, others to be classes or chiefs of angels. Scholars note that this number was a trial for the disbelievers, a certainty for the People of the Book and an increase in faith for the believers.

This verse describes what went through the mind of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira when he heard the Qur'an: he reflected on it and prepared in his heart a statement to disparage it, and God cursed him for that preparation. Then he looked around, frowned, scowled, turned away and grew arrogant, and said: "This is nothing but magic transmitted from others, this is nothing but the word of a human." Commentators agree that the verse portrays the man and the aims of those who sought to discredit revelation, and that the phrase "he was cursed, how he planned" is either a curse or a blame. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate the occasion of revelation: the Quraysh pressed al-Walid to say something against the Qur'an, and he said it resembled neither poetry, nor soothsaying, nor madness, but had sweetness and grandeur. Ibn Kathir takes the aim to be his denial that it came from God. Al-Zamakhshari gives several readings of "how he planned": an expression of amazement at the accuracy of his remark, a sarcastic praise, or a quotation of the Quraysh's mocking words, a view Ibn 'Atiyya also considers. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan explain that "qutila" means cursed or overcome, and that the repetition with "thumma" intensifies the rebuke. On "yu'thar", al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi understand "narrated from another", while Abu Hayyan suggests "preferred". Ibn 'Ashur concludes that this speech, born of hesitation, aimed to deny that the Qur'an is a divine revelation.

The commentators explain that this verse is part of the description of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who was granted wealth, sons and status by God and then obstinately opposed the verses of the Qur'an. The phrase (fa-qutila kayfa qaddara) means, in the usual explanation, that he was cursed or punished for how he prepared his false words in his mind. The commentators agree that al-Walid reflected on the Qur'an and arranged what he would say about it, then looked around, frowned and scowled, then turned away in arrogance and declared that the Qur'an is only transmitted magic and merely human speech rather than the word of God. Most agree that the repetition of "then he was cursed" is for emphasis, and that "then" signals that the second curse is stronger than the first.

They differ over the meaning of "qutila". Al-Zuhri took it to mean punished, others understood it as cursed, and others as subdued and humbled. Al-Zamakhshari suggested it could be ironic praise or a quotation of the Quraysh's own words, and read it as a sign of his wretched state. Ibn 'Atiyya considered that it might express praise for his first admiration of the Qur'an, in the manner of an Arabic exclamation of wonder. Al-Tabari read it as astonishment, disbelief and reproach.

According to the reports, al-Walid made this declaration after Abu Jahl and the Quraysh pressed him to find a word that would satisfy them, having first denied poetry, soothsaying and madness. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain his words as magic handed down from others, without settling the question of the sources named, which include Musaylima and the people of Babylon.

The commentators explain this verse as part of the story of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, who reflected on the Quran he had heard from the Prophet ﷺ and prepared in his mind what he would say about it. For this calculation he earned the curse, after which he frowned, turned away arrogantly and said: this is only transmitted magic, this is only the speech of a human. Most exegetes agree that qutila means he was cursed or that destruction was called upon him, the repetition serving emphasis, and that thumma indicates the second curse is stronger than the first. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir present the Walid's reflections and his hostility as the setting, while al-Baghawi and Ibn Sa'di read the curse as directed at his deliberate fabrication. Al-Zuhri holds that qutila means he was punished, and others say it means he was overcome and humbled. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan suggest instead that the phrase expresses wonder at the sharpness of his thinking, or an ironic praise, or a mocking echo of what the Quraysh said. Ibn 'Ashur reads kayfa qaddara as an interrogative of astonishment mixed with reproach, and sees the verse as a progression in his rejection. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi preserve the narration of the Quraysh's attempt to discredit the Prophet through him.

These verses describe al-Walid ibn al-Mughira's reflection on the Quran and the stubborn rejection that followed. According to the commentators, he pondered and planned what to say about the Quran, then looked around at the people or searched for something with which to attack it. Finding no opening, he frowned and his face grew sour; he turned away from the truth, grew arrogant, and declared that the Quran was merely sorcery handed down from others, the speech of humans and not the word of God. The exegetes agree that these verses were revealed concerning al-Walid, and that the word fa-qutila means he was cursed, the repetition serving emphasis. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that he was nicknamed al-Wahid, and that the verses recall his wealth, sons and standing, yet his hostility only grew. Al-Tabari understands nazara as reflection and deliberation, while Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri take it as a second look, and al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi as a glance at the people or at what might repel the Quran. On the meaning of basara, Qatada and Ibn Kathir say it means a sour, contorted face, al-Suddi a change of expression, and al-Razi distinguishes a frown before the debate from a scowl after it. As for sa'ud, most take it as a grueling ascent or a mountain of fire in hell, transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, while others read it as a hardship without relief. Opinions also differ on the nineteen guardians of the fire, whom most take to be angels, while al-Tha'alibi allows that they could be categories, ranks or chiefs.

These verses describe al-Walid ibn al-Mughira's reaction when he reflected on the Qur'an and prepared in his heart what he would say about it. Then he looked around at the people, frowned and scowled, having found no fault to criticise, before turning away and showing arrogance towards the truth. The commentators agree that these verses were revealed about him. On the meaning of 'abasa' and 'basara', most explain that the first is the knitting of the brows and the second the tightening and changing of the face, and al-Sam'ani considers that both words carry the same sense, as happens to a person troubled by a matter who reflects on it at length. The reports relate that al-Walid said the Qur'an is neither poetry, nor soothsaying, nor madness, that it has sweetness and beauty, that it rises and is not surpassed, and then called it a magic he received from others. Ibn Zayd and Abu Razin say he took it from others, while as-Suddi reports it was attributed to a slave of a Hadrami clan, and others to Musaylima or to the people of Babylon. As for 'qutila kayfa qaddara', most take it as a curse, al-Zuhri as a punishment, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya consider it may be praise of his first admiration. Finally, the mention of Saqar as a name of Hell and of the nineteen guardians prompts various explanations recorded by al-Mawardi and others.

These verses describe al-Walid ibn al-Mughira's reflection on the Quran he heard from the Prophet ﷺ, how he pondered and prepared his words in his mind, then frowned and scowled, turned away from the truth in arrogance, and declared that the Quran is only magic transmitted from others and mere human speech rather than God's word. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree that the verses were revealed about this man, and that the curse in 'then he was cursed, how he planned' is a rebuke and a condemnation of his conduct rather than a mere wish. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate accounts that he was first impressed by the Quran and then called it sorcery under pressure from Abu Jahl. Al-Razi argues that his frown shows he knew the Prophet was truthful and was merely stubborn, while others distinguish between 'abasa and basara as stages of expression. On the phrase 'yu'thar', al-Tabari and al-Nasafi take it as 'transmitted from others', while al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy also note the sense of 'preferred'. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi identify the guardians of Hell as angels, and al-Razi explains the number nineteen as one that combines the smallest many and the largest few. Regarding 'sa'ud', Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as a heavy burden of punishment, whereas Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports it as a mountain of fire.

This passage tells of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who reflected on the Qur'an and prepared in his mind what to say about it, then frowned, scowled, turned away and grew arrogant, and said: "This is nothing but transmitted magic, nothing but the word of a human being." The commentators agree that these verses were revealed concerning him and that the threat of punishment targets his stubbornness and this statement. All read "qutila" as a curse, repeated for emphasis, though al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note it may also express wonder or ironic praise. Al-Zamakhshari observes that "thumma" here marks an escalation to a stronger stage. For "sa'udan", most explain it as a painful punishment, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri is cited in a hadith describing a mountain of fire that he must climb, a report not accepted by all. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid put his wealth at a thousand dinars or more, 'Umar took it as a monthly income, and the number of his sons varies in the reports from seven to thirteen. On "yu'thar", most say it means "narrated from others", while some understand it as "preferred over all other magic". Al-Razi argues that his frowning shows he inwardly knew the Prophet was truthful but denied out of obstinacy, though others do not draw this conclusion. Overall, the verses link obstinacy to its punishment and affirm that guidance and misguidance rest with God.

The commentators explain that this verse closes al-Walid ibn al-Mughira's remarks about the Qur'an, in which he claims it is merely human speech and not the word of God. It repeats and confirms the previous phrase, 'this is only magic handed down.' Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the Qur'an is human utterance rather than divine speech. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi add that al-Walid borrowed it from someone else; some name a servant of the Banu al-Hadrami, others Musaylima, the people of Babylon, or a soothsayer. Nearly all report that he first reflected and then spoke. Al-Razi notes that if the charge were true, the Arabs, who share the same language, could have answered it, and he argues that al-Walid spoke out of obstinacy rather than conviction, since he had admitted the Qur'an's sweetness. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur see the restrictive wording as a conclusion reached after deliberation. Abu Hayyan, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the sentence reinforces the one before it without a connecting particle. Al-Alusi attributes his stance to pride and to the hostility of his people. The commentators agree that the verse is a condemnation and a belittling of the claim, and that it leads into the threat that follows.

This verse says that God will cast the one described, whom most commentators identify as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, into Saqar, a name of Hell. Ibn Abbas counts it as the sixth level, though others say the fifth, and the commentators agree it is a proper name for Hell that takes no nunation. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada explain that Saqar leaves no one alive and no one dead, since bodies are burned and renewed again and again. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya add that it destroys everything thrown into it. The word lawwaha is read in the nominative by most and in the accusative by a few readers. Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to mean that the fire scorches and blackens the skin, while al-Hasan, Ibn Kaysan and al-Razi take it to mean that Hell becomes visible from afar. Most commentators say the nineteen are angelic guardians, and al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir describe them as the most formidable of the angels. Others read them as categories, ranks or chiefs of angels. Many commentators, including al-Tabari and al-Baghawi, say the number was a trial for the disbelievers who mocked it, a confirmation for the People of the Book who find it in their scriptures, and an increase in faith for believers. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur also propose symbolic readings without deciding among them.

The commentators explain that God addresses the Prophet with a question meant to magnify and terrify: what is Saqar? The verse then describes it as a fire that leaves nothing alive and spares nothing that is cast into it. Nearly all agree that Saqar is a name for Hell or for one of its levels, and that the word is feminine and indeclinable. On the phrase 'it leaves nothing and spares nothing', al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd report that the fire neither kills nor gives life, so that the damned are burned again each time their bodies are renewed. Al-Suddi takes it to mean that it leaves neither flesh nor bone, while Ibn Kathir and others see mere emphasis in the repetition. The description 'scorching the skin' is, according to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and most scholars, a reference to a fire that blackens and burns the skin, the word basharmeaning skin. Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan read it as a fire visible to people from afar, while al-Akhfash takes it to mean something that causes thirst. As for the nineteen guardians, most commentators understand nineteen angels, while others speak of nineteen categories or ranks. Al-Razi, al-Mawardi and others offer symbolic reasons for this number, but none of them settles the matter definitively.

This verse describes the Fire called Saqar, which, according to the commentators, leaves nothing alive and nothing dead. Mujahid explains that it neither lets those within die nor lets them live, burning them each time their skins are renewed. Al-Suddi says it leaves no flesh and no bone, while al-Dahhak says that once it seizes people it leaves none of them whole, and that when they are restored it does not spare them until it consumes them. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud explain that it lets nothing cast into it survive, and that whatever is thrown into it is inevitably destroyed. Most scholars hold that the two phrases have the same meaning and are repeated for emphasis, whereas al-Razi offers several ways of distinguishing them. As for lawwaha lil-bashar, the majority, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, understand it as scorching and blackening the skin; al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan take it to mean that the Fire becomes visible to people from afar, and al-Akhfash that it parches them with thirst. All agree that nineteen keepers are in charge of it. Some take them to be nineteen named angels, others nineteen categories or ranks, the first view being the most widespread. The commentators also note that this number was a trial for the disbelievers, a confirmation for the People of the Book and an increase in faith for the believers, and that the passage was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who reflected on the Qur'an and then declared it magic and mere human speech.

This verse describes Saqar, a level of Hell that leaves nothing of those cast into it and spares none, consuming them and then restoring them so the punishment continues. The commentators broadly agree that "lawwaha lil-bashar" means that it alters and blackens the skin and burns its surface. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Razin and most scholars say it scorches the skin until it is blacker than night, while Qatada and Zayd ibn Aslam stress the burning. "Al-bashar" is the plural of "bashara", the outer skin for most, although al-Akhfash takes it to mean the damned humans. Al-Hasan, Ibn Kaysan and al-Asamm read "lawwaha" as "shining out": the fire becomes visible to people from five hundred years away, a view also attributed to Ibn 'Abbas. Some read "lawwahatan" in the accusative for emphasis. As for "over it are nineteen", most commentators identify them as the nineteen angelic guardians of Hell, while others take them to be nineteen categories, ranks or chiefs. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi relate that Abu Jahl mocked this number before the Quraysh, which led to the following verse being revealed.

This verse states that Hell, called Saqar, is guarded by nineteen angels who hold authority over it and over its people. The commentators explain that the phrase "scorching the human skin" means that it blackens and burns the skin and leaves nothing of those thrown into it, yet re-creates them so that the punishment never ends. They agree that the number refers to the guardians, and that these angels are of great strength and harshness, which is why mercy does not move them. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that when the verse was revealed Abu Jahl told the Quraysh that ten of them could overpower one guard, and Abu al-Ashadd al-Jumahi boasted that he alone would push back many of them; the Qur'an responds to this mockery. Al-Razi offers several symbolic reasons for the number, drawn from human faculties, the gates of Hell or the hours of the day, but commits to none of them, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi prefer to leave its wisdom to God. Al-Tabari and al-Shinqiti take the word "fitna" as a test: the People of the Book would find the number in their scriptures and grow certain, believers would grow in faith, while those with sickness in their hearts and the disbelievers would ask what God meant. Readers differ on the form of the number, with some reciters dropping a vowel in the second part, and a few rare readings are noted by Ibn Jinni and others.

This passage describes the keepers of Hell as angels of great strength, and explains that the stated number of nineteen was a trial for the disbelievers, who mocked it, such as Abu Jahl and Abu al-Ashudd. Commentators agree that the announcement was meant to bring the People of the Book to certainty, since the Qur'an matched what was in their scriptures, and to increase the faith of the believers, so that neither the People of the Book nor the believers would doubt. The hypocrites and the disbelievers then ask what God intended by this example. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the verse was revealed in response to Abu Jahl, who claimed that ten men from Quraysh could overpower one of the guardians; this account is transmitted notably through Ibn Abbas and Qatada. Most exegetes take the 'disease in the heart' to mean hypocrisy, which raises a problem since the sura is Meccan; they answer that it foretells what would happen in Medina. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl instead understands it as doubt rather than hypocrisy. All agree that God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, that none knows the hosts of your Lord but Him, and that Hell is a reminder to mankind. Commentators differ on what 'it' refers to: Saqar according to some, the verses or the number according to others. Several acknowledge that the precise wisdom behind the number is known to God alone.

God swears by the moon, by the night as it turns away, and by the dawn as it brightens, that Hell is one of the greatest of calamities and a warning to mankind. The commentators explain that each person may choose to advance toward obedience and faith, or to fall back into disobedience, since the warning has reached everyone. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak understand “al-kubar” as Hell, while Ibn Abbas reads it as a grave sin or as the severity of denying the Prophet. Al-Hasan said no warning was ever more dreadful than the fire. Ibn Zayd took the “nadhir” to be the Prophet Muhammad, while Abu Razin took it to be God Himself. Most commentators take the pronoun in “innaha” to refer to Hell. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read “kalla” as a rebuke to those who deny this warning, while al-Tabari reads it as a rejection of the claim that people could withstand the guardians of Hell. On the two readings “idh adbara” and “idha dabara”, al-Tabari and most scholars hold that they are two dialects with the same meaning, while some linguists distinguish “dabara” as coming after or following behind.

In this verse God swears by the moon, by the night as it turns away, and by the dawn as it brightens, to affirm the magnitude of Hell, which the commentators describe as one of the greatest calamities. They agree that the pronoun "it" refers to Hell, that "al-kubar" means great catastrophes, and that "nadhiran" means a warner that frightens people, which some read as a state or a specifier. The readings differ: Nafi', Hamza, Hafs and Ya'qub read "idh adbara", while others read "idha dabara". Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda hold that dabara and adbara are one in meaning, like qabila and aqbala, whereas Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba distinguish them, taking dabara to mean came after and adbara to mean turned away. Al-Tabari concludes that both readings are correct. Regarding "for whoever of you wishes to advance or delay", Ibn Jurayj takes it as advancing in obedience to God and delaying from disobedience, al-Suddi as advancing toward the Fire or delaying from Paradise, and Yahya ibn Sallam as advancing toward good or delaying toward evil. As for "every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned", the companions of the right are excepted: Ibn 'Abbas identifies them with the angels, 'Ali with the children of Muslims, and al-Hasan with sincere believers.

In this verse God swears by the dawn when it breaks and its darkness is dispelled. This oath follows the oaths by the moon and by the night as it withdraws, and its answer is that the Fire is one of the greatest calamities. The commentators agree that the pronoun "it" refers to Hell (Saqar), mentioned just before, and that "asfara" means to shine forth and become clear. Al-Hasan al-Basri says that God has never warned mankind of anything more terrible than it, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as Hell itself.

Opinions differ on the phrase "a warner to mankind". Al-Hasan, Abu Razin and Muqatil take it as a description of the Fire itself, and Abu Razin even takes it as God's own words. Ibn Zayd identifies it with the Prophet Muhammad, while al-Zamakhshari treats it as a qualifier or a separate clause. Al-Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya and most grammarians read it as a circumstantial accusative, a specification, or a verbal noun meaning a warning. For the phrase "for whoever among you wills to go forward or to fall back", Ibn Jurayj explains it as going forward in obedience to God or falling back from disobedience, al-Suddi as going forward toward the Fire or falling back toward Paradise, and Yahya ibn Salam as advancing toward good or sliding toward evil. Al-Hasan reads it as a warning, similar to the verse "whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve".

On the reading of "adbara" and "dabara", Abu Ubayda, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba hold that the two forms are synonyms, while Abu Ubayda and some linguists distinguish between them, taking "dabara" to mean following behind and "adbara" to mean turning away. Finally, al-Tabari takes the opening "kalla" as a rejection of the claim that one could withstand the guardians of Hell, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as a denial that Hell could be a reminder to them.

God swears by the moon, by the night as it turns away, and by the dawn as it brightens, that Hell, Saqar, is one of the greatest calamities, and that it is a warning to mankind. The commentators agree that the pronoun "it" refers to the Fire and that "the greatest" means great calamities and severe torments; al-Kalbi and Muqatil specify that these are the seven levels of Hell. On the meaning of "adbara" and "dabara", al-Farra', al-Akhfash and Tha'lab hold that the two forms are synonymous, while Abu 'Ubayda distinguishes them, taking dabara to mean "to come after" and adbara to mean "to turn away". As for the warner, al-Hasan says the Fire has never warned people of anything more dreadful, Abu Razin says God Himself is the warner, and Ibn Zayd says it is the Prophet ﷺ, who is commanded to rise and warn. In the phrase "for whoever of you wishes to go forward or fall back", Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj understand going forward as obedience and falling back as disobedience, al-Suddi understands it as going towards the Fire or away from it towards Paradise, and al-Hasan takes it as a threat like "whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve". Regarding the "companions of the right" mentioned next, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan identify them as sincere believers, 'Ali as the children of Muslims, and Ibn 'Abbas as the angels. The exegetes thus agree on the warning and the gravity of the Fire, but differ on who the warner is and on the meaning of going forward and falling back.

The commentators explain that “nadhīran lil-bashar” means that the Fire, one of the great calamities, is a warning to mankind, meant to awaken them. They differ on who is the warner. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Zayd, reports that some take it to be the Prophet ﷺ, commanded to warn, while Abu Razin sees God as the one who warns. Al-Hasan al-Basri states that God never warned mankind with anything more dreadful than the Fire. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also note that Mujahid and others understood “hiya” to refer to the Fire described just before.

On the word “al-kubar”, al-Baghawi, al-Tha'alibi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that Muqatil and al-Kalbi take it to mean the seven levels of Hell. Regarding “liman sha'a minkum an yataqaddama aw yata'akhkhara”, most scholars, including Ibn Juzayy and al-Tabari, read advancing as moving toward obedience and lagging as turning toward disobedience. Al-Hasan sees here a threat similar to “whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve”, while al-Qurtubi and al-Mawardi mention other views, such as the reading that the will belongs to God. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur discuss how the phrase relates to human will, but the commentators do not settle the matter beyond noting the choice.

The commentators agree that the warning has reached everyone, believers and disbelievers alike, and that each person bears responsibility for his choice. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi note that the oath by the moon, the retreating night and the dawn that appears evokes the contrast between guidance and misguidance. Ibn al-Qayyim adds reflections on these signs of God's power.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a divine oath that follows the word "kalla", and that its meaning is as follows: Hell, described as one of the greatest calamities, is a warning to mankind. Whoever among them wishes to advance toward obedience and faith, or to fall back into disobedience and disbelief, is free to do so. Most agree on this reading: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that "to advance" means to hasten toward obedience to God, and "to fall behind" means to hold back from it. Al-Suddi takes it to refer to the Fire and the Garden: advancing toward the Fire and lagging behind from the Garden. Al-Zajjaj applies it to the commands one should carry out and the prohibitions one should avoid.

Opinions differ on what the pronoun in "innaha" refers to. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say it is Hell; others say it is the warning, the Hereafter, or the surah itself. As for "nadhiran", al-Hasan holds that the Fire is itself the warner, and that no people were ever warned by anything more dreadful. Ibn Zayd takes it to be the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Razin takes it to be God, and others take it to be the Quran, or a grammatical complement.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy consider "for whoever wills" to be an apposition to "to mankind", while Ibn Atiyya and al-Hasan read it as a threat similar to the verse "whoever wills, let him believe; whoever wills, let him disbelieve". Al-Razi reports that the Mu'tazila cite this verse to affirm human freedom, and that the Ash'aris reply that human will depends on God's will.

The commentators explain that every soul is held in pledge by what it has earned, confined before God by its deeds, good or bad, and will not be released until it has received its due. They agree on the exception introduced by "except the companions of the right," who are not held by their sins, but they differ on who these are. Ali, as reported by al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, and followed by al-Farra', identified them as the children of Muslims, who have no sins. Ibn Abbas, in the transmission of Abu Dhabyan, took them to be the angels, while al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan took them to be sincere Muslims who had fulfilled their obligations. Muqatil linked them to the people of Paradise who stood on Adam's right at the covenant, al-Dahhak to those for whom the best reward had been decreed, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understood them as those who freed themselves by their good deeds.

On the question "what brought you into Saqar?", the commentators report that the damned answer that they did not pray, did not feed the poor, plunged into vain talk with the plungers, and denied the Day of Judgment until certainty came upon them, meaning death. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi add that intercession does not benefit disbelievers. None of the authors settles the disagreement; they simply report each view as transmitted.

The commentators explain that the verse states every soul is held in pledge by what it has earned, meaning it remains bound by its misdeeds unless it frees itself through obedience. The exception is the People of the Right, who are not held by their sins because God forgives and overlooks them, and who dwell in gardens where they ask one another about the criminals. The exegetes agree on the central contrast between the fate of believers and that of those who deny, but differ on who the People of the Right are. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Umar, al-Farra' and Ibn Kathir take them to be the children of Muslims. Ibn Abbas, in the transmission of Abu Dhabyan, says they are the angels. Al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Ibn Kaysan and Abu al-Su'ud say they are sincere Muslims or believers. Muqatil identifies them with those who stood at Adam's right on the Day of the Covenant, and others with those who receive their record in their right hand. As for the criminals, they list four failings that brought them to Saqar: not praying, not feeding the needy, plunging into vain talk with the plungers, and denying the Day of Judgement. Qatada explains plunging as following every misguided person into error, al-Suddi as denying along with the deniers, and Ibn Zayd as their accusations against the Prophet of being a soothsayer, a madman, a poet or a sorcerer. Al-Zamakhshari sees the question as a rebuke, and the placing of the denial of Judgement last as a way of stressing its gravity. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi understand the certainty as death.

This verse says that every soul is held in pledge by what it has earned with God, except the people of the right, who are in gardens where they ask one another about the criminals and what brought them into Saqar. The commentators agree that the criminals are the disbelievers and polytheists, and that their answer lists the essential failings: not praying, not feeding the poor, plunging into empty talk with those who babble in falsehood, and denying the Day of Judgment until death came. The commentators differ on who the people of the right are. Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Umar identified them as the children of Muslims, Ibn Abbas in one report as the angels, al-Dahhak as believers to whom the best reward had been promised, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan as sincere Muslims, while al-Kalbi and Muqatil described them as those who stood at Adam's right hand on the day of the covenant. There is also a debate about who is questioned: some say the blessed ask the damned directly, others that they ask the angels about their relatives. As for the word khawd, Qatada took it to mean following every misguided person, al-Suddi denial, and Ibn Zayd the accusations against the Prophet of being a soothsayer, poet or sorcerer. On intercession, the exegetes agree that it will not benefit the disbelievers, though several note that it will benefit others on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Ashur observes that the present tense in their words shows that this was their habit throughout life.

This passage states that every soul is held in pledge by what it has earned, and is not released until it has paid what it owes, except the people of the right, whose pledge is redeemed by their good deeds, as a debtor frees his pledge by paying his due. They are in gardens where they ask one another about the criminals: "What brought you into Saqar?" The criminals answer that they were not among those who pray, did not feed the needy, used to plunge into vain talk with the vain, and denied the Day of Judgment until certainty came to them, meaning death. The commentators differ on who the people of the right are. Ali and others say they are the children of Muslims, who have no sins; Ibn Abbas, in one report, says they are the angels; al-Dahhak says they are those for whom the good reward was decreed; al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan say they are sincere Muslims who fulfilled their duties. On the meaning of plunging, Qatada says whenever an astray person went astray they went astray with him; al-Suddi says it means denying along with the deniers; Ibn Zayd says it means their claims about the Prophet, calling him a soothsayer, a magician and a poet. On intercession, the commentators agree it does not benefit disbelievers, and Ibn Mas'ud reports that angels, prophets, martyrs and the righteous will intercede, leaving some in the Fire. The passage then describes those who turn away from the reminder as wild donkeys fleeing a lion or archers; for the commentators, their demand for unrolled scrolls is stubbornness rather than lack of proof. The Qur'an is a reminder from which whoever wills may benefit, and God is worthy of fear and worthy of forgiveness.

This part of the verse describes the people of the Garden asking the criminals, who are in Saqar, what brought them into the Fire. The criminals answer that they did not pray, did not feed the poor, plunged into falsehood with those who plunged, and denied the Day of Judgment until death reached them. The commentators agree that Saqar is Hell and that the answer lists the chief causes of ruin. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that khawd means engaging in falsehood and following every deviator, as Qatada says. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi record several readings, such as denying the Prophet, or calling him a soothsayer, poet or sorcerer, as as-Suddi and Ibn Zayd hold. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take yaqin to mean death, while noting it may also mean the certainty gained after death of what they had denied. Al-Zamakhshari sees the question as a rebuke and reproach rather than true ignorance, and holds that disbelievers are addressed by the legal duties. Al-Razi draws from the verse that disbelievers are punished for neglecting the branches of the law, and that intercession benefits some. Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Mas'ud, adds that intercession will not benefit these people.

This verse describes how every soul is held in pledge by what it earned on the Day of Judgment, except the people of the right hand, who are freed and dwell in gardens, asking one another about the criminals: what brought you into Saqar? The criminals reply that they were not among those who prayed, did not feed the poor, plunged into falsehood along with the plungers, and denied the Day of Judgment until certainty, meaning death, came to them, as most commentators explain. The commentators agree that these four faults are the roots of the sins that lead to the Fire, and that neglecting prayer and charity, vain talk and denying the Judgment are among the gravest. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur take prayer and charity as the obligatory ones, while al-Nasafi and al-Alusi read it as belief in their obligation, and some scholars cite the passage to argue that unbelievers are bound by the legal duties. On the people of the right hand, Ali ibn Abi Talib and those who follow him say they are the children of Muslims, Ibn Abbas in one report says the angels, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan say sincere believers, and al-Dahhak says believers. As for the word for plunging, Qatada explains it as following every deviator into his deviation, al-Suddi as denying along with the deniers, and Ibn Zayd as the slanders of soothsayer, madman, sorcerer and poet directed at the Prophet. All agree that intercession will not benefit these criminals, and some draw from this that it will benefit other monotheists. The commentators also differ on the meaning of the frightened donkeys and the qaswara, understood variously as archers, a lion, or the noise of a crowd.

The commentators explain that this verse is part of the dialogue between the people of Paradise and the criminals in the Fire. The companions of the right ask what brought the guilty into Saqar, and they answer that they did not pray, did not feed the needy, plunged into vain talk with the other sinners, and denied the Day of Judgement until certainty, meaning death, came to them. The shared reading is that these four conduct are the cause of the punishment, and that these words are spoken after the guilty have seen their fate. Scholars differ on who the companions of the right are. Ali ibn Abi Talib, and in one report Ibn Abbas, identify them as the children of Muslims; Ibn Abbas in another report identifies them as the angels; al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kaysan take them to be sincere believers who fulfilled their duties; and al-Baqir takes them to be his own followers. On the failure to pray and feed the poor, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy understand obligatory prayer and zakat, and al-Razi and al-Qurtubi use the verse to argue that unbelievers are bound by the rules of the law, whereas al-Zamakhshari holds that the verse concerns only unbelievers. Qatada explains the immersion in falsehood as each deviant leading his followers astray, and Ibn Zayd explains it as the slander against the Prophet of being a soothsayer, a poet or a sorcerer. Most exegetes take the certainty to be death, while Ibn Atiyya understands it as the truth of what they denied, namely resurrection. Nearly all agree that intercession will not benefit these criminals, though it is affirmed for others.

This verse states that every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned, except the people of the right hand, who are freed by their deeds and are in gardens asking the guilty: what brought you into Saqar? The guilty reply that they did not pray, did not feed the poor, plunged into falsehood with those who plunged, and denied the Day of Judgement until death came upon them. Commentators agree that khawd means engaging in falsehood and idle talk, and that denying the Day of Judgement is the gravest offence, mentioned last to magnify it, as al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note. Al-Tabari and Qatada explain that whoever went astray, they went astray with him, al-Suddi says they denied with the deniers, and Ibn Zayd reports that they called the Prophet a soothsayer, a madman, a poet or a sorcerer. As for the people of the right hand, opinions differ: Ali holds that they are the children of Muslims, Ibn Abbas that they are angels, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan that they are sincere believers, and al-Dahhak that they are those not held in pledge. Al-Zamakhshari reads rahina as a noun meaning a pledge rather than a feminine adjective, and the release as achieved by good deeds. Ibn Kathir and others hold that intercession does not benefit disbelievers, whereas al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy derive from the verse proof that intercession benefits others. Most commentators take qaswara to mean archers, while others take it to mean a lion. The readings differ on mustanfira between the vowels a and i, and the passage ends with the mention of God's will.

This passage describes a dialogue between the people of the Fire and those of the Garden. Asked what brought them into Saqar, they reply that they did not pray, did not feed the needy, plunged into vain talk with the wrongdoers, and denied the Day of Judgement, until certainty came to them. Most commentators, including Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sudi and Ibn Kathir, take 'certainty' to mean death. Ibn 'Atiyya disagrees: he reads it as the reality of what they denied, namely the return to God and the Hereafter, since death itself is a certainty even for the disbeliever while still alive, and he cites the verse 'Worship your Lord until certainty comes to you'. All agree that the intercession of intercessors does not benefit the disbelievers, and al-Razi, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take this to imply that intercession does benefit others. As for the 'companions of the right', al-Tabari reports from Ali that they are the children of Muslims, Ibn 'Abbas says they are the angels, al-Hasan identifies them as sincere Muslims, and al-Zamakhshari as believers who freed themselves by their good deeds. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the denial of the Day of Judgement is mentioned last to stress its gravity. On the word 'qaswara', Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid say it means archers, while Abu Hurayra and most philologists say it means a lion, and Ibn 'Abbas also gives the sense of the noise of people. Al-Tabari explains the verse as describing those who turn away from the Qur'an as wild asses flee a hunter, who want scriptures sent down to them personally, and the answer that they do not fear the Hereafter, and that the Qur'an is a reminder which whoever wills may heed.

This part of the verse describes the people of the left, who in the Fire are asked what brought them into Saqar. They list four causes: they did not pray, they did not feed the poor, they plunged into vain talk with the frivolous, and they denied the Day of Judgment, until the certainty came to them. Nearly all commentators, including al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn, take the certainty to mean death. Ibn 'Atiyya disagrees: in his view the certainty is the truth of what they denied, namely the return to God and the afterlife, which they recognise only after death, since death itself is already a certainty for the living. Regarding the next phrase, that no intercession will benefit them, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi see it as a denial of intercession for disbelievers, while Ibn Mas'ud, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi report that angels, prophets, martyrs and believers will intercede for sinners who are monotheists, and al-Razi notes that the exclusion implies others will benefit. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari discuss the seriousness of neglecting prayer, which al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi tie to obligatory prayer and charity. Ibn 'Ashur explains that these four are the root causes of ruin, and he notes that the verse does not settle whether disbelievers are bound by the legal duties of the Sharia.

This verse states that the intercession of intercessors will not benefit the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment. Its context describes the people of the right, who are saved, asking the criminals what brought them into Saqar. The criminals answer that they did not pray, did not feed the poor, plunged into vain talk with the plungers, and denied the Day of Judgment until certainty, meaning death, came to them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the intercessors, angels, prophets, martyrs and believers, will intercede for the believers, while the disbelievers have no intercessor. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy conclude that the denial is a punishment for those not approved by God. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur draw the opposite inference, that intercession benefits others. Scholars differ on the people of the right: Ali and al-Farra identify them as children of Muslims, Ibn Abbas as angels, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan as sincere believers, and Ibn Jurayj as those who will not be called to account. On certainty, most exegetes take it to be death, while Ibn Atiyya understands it as the reality they had denied, which they witness after death. Al-Shinqiti notes that intercession happens only with God's permission.

This verse asks, in a tone of rebuke and wonder, why the disbelievers turn away from the reminder, meaning the admonition of the Quran and its lessons. Most commentators, including Qatada and Ibn Kathir, understand the reminder to be the Quran, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya widen it to include any admonition. The word 'mu'ridin' is a circumstantial state, and some take it to mean that they became averse. It follows the preceding passage, in which the wrongdoers, asked about their fate, say that they did not pray, did not feed the needy, plunged into vain talk with the vain, and denied the Day of Judgment, until 'the certainty' came, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take to be death. Their flight is compared to wild donkeys fleeing in terror. Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra and Zayd ibn Aslam take 'al-qaswara' to mean the lion, while Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to mean archers; others say it means human noises or the darkness of night. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir stress that the comparison is a strong rebuke. Commentators agree that the two readings of 'mustanfira', with fatha or kasra, carry closely related meanings.

The commentators explain that God rebukes those who turn away from the Quranic reminder and compares them, in their flight, to wild donkeys panicked by a lion or by archers. The readings of "mustanfira" differ: Nafi' and Ibn Amir read it with a fatha on the fa', meaning "driven away," while the rest read it with a kasra, meaning "fleeing." Al-Farra' says both forms are common in Arabic, while al-Razi prefers the kasra because the following verb "fled" shows that the animals themselves took flight. As for "qaswara," the commentators offer several views: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say it means archers, Abu Hurayra, Zayd ibn Aslam and Ata' say it means the lion, and others say it means the noise of people, a band of men, or the darkness at the start of night. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that Ibn Abbas said the lion is called qaswara in Ethiopic. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the basic meaning remains the same: these idolaters flee the truth as the donkeys flee danger. On the verse about wanting unrolled scrolls, most commentators, including Qatada, al-Kalbi, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi, report that they demanded a written document from heaven confirming the Prophet's mission, while Abu Salih mentions a release from Hell. All agree that God rejects this demand with "kalla," and that the real cause of their refusal is their lack of fear of the Hereafter, as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir then stress that the Quran is a reminder, that remembering it depends on God's will, and that God deserves to be feared and to forgive, citing a hadith from Anas.

The verse describes the idolaters who turn away from the Qur'an, likening them to wild donkeys in panic fleeing from something that frightens them. The commentators differ on the meaning of "qaswara". Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ikrima take it to mean archers or hunters, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr identifies them as huntsmen and Abu Hurayra, Zayd ibn Aslam and Ata' take it to mean the lion, as does al-Kalbi. Ibn Abbas is reported in different versions, sometimes saying it is the lion, sometimes the archers, and al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi cite his statement that the word means the lion in Ethiopian. Others understand it as the noise of people, a band of strong men, or the darkness at the start of night. All agree that the comparison is meant to disparage the unbelievers and expose their folly. The reading "mustanfira" with a kasra means "fleeing", while with a fatha it means "startled"; al-Farisi prefers the kasra and Abu Ubayd the fatha. Several exegetes report that the Quraysh demanded that each of them receive a scripture from heaven, and God rejects this with "kalla". According to Qatada, the real reason for their refusal is their lack of fear of the Hereafter. The apparent meaning these commentators retain is thus a flight from the reminder.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the description of the unbelievers turning away from the reminder, and that their aversion does not stem from a lack of evidence but from stubbornness and unreasonable demands. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that each of them wanted a book sent down from God ordering him to believe in Muhammad ﷺ, as a kind of challenge; al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi add that some wanted a sheet guaranteeing their freedom from the Fire without any deeds. Al-Kalbi mentions a practice attributed to the Children of Israel, in which each person's sin was written at his head, but al-Tabari does not adopt this explanation. All agree that the divine reply, "kalla", rejects this wish, and that the real cause of their refusal is their lack of fear of the Hereafter, as stated by Qatada, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. Al-Zamakhshari explains that "munashshara" means open sheets that can be read, and that Ibn Jubayr read the word with a lighter form without changing its meaning. Al-Farra' reports another context in which the Quraysh compared this to what was said of the Children of Israel. Some, such as al-Jalalayn, simply state that it refers to a book from God ordering them to follow the Prophet.

This verse answers those who turned away from the Qur'an and demanded that a book be sent down from heaven to each of them individually. The commentators explain that "kallā" is a rebuke that rejects this demand. The real reason for their turning away is not that they cannot believe what has come to them, but that they do not fear the Hereafter and do not believe in resurrection or reward, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state.

Most exegetes read the verse as part of the description of the fate of the wrongdoers, and hold that their disregard of the Hereafter explains their refusal of the message. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate that this demand for a personal book came from leaders of Quraysh, and that the Prophet did not grant it. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress that obstinacy, not any lack of evidence, is what drives this attitude.

The commentators differ on the meaning of "kallā" itself. Al-Baghawi and al-Sam'ani sometimes take it to mean "truly," while most, including al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud, read it as a rejection that dismisses the claim. Ibn 'Ashur explains that denying their fear of the Hereafter amounts to saying they do not believe in the life to come. No commentary decides between these readings.

This verse states that the Qur'an is a reminder and a sufficient, powerful admonition: whoever wills may remember and be guided by it, yet such remembrance happens only by God's will. The commentators agree that the opening word "no" rejects the demand of the disbelievers who asked for unrolled scrolls sent down from heaven, and that the pronoun "it" refers to the Qur'an or to what has preceded. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that people can remember only if God enables them, and Ibn Kathir compares this with the verse "You will not will except that God wills." Al-Zamakhshari reads God's will as a compulsion that forces people to remember, an interpretation the Mu'tazilites upheld, which al-Razi rejects on the ground that remembrance is denied absolutely except when the will intervenes. All agree that God is worthy to be feared and worthy to forgive those who fear Him. Several cite a hadith of Anas on this point, which Ibn Kathir and others regard as weak in its chain, in which God declares that He deserves to be feared and not to be associated with. As for the "unrolled scrolls," al-Baghawi and al-Tabari take them as letters from God addressed to each man by name, while al-Zamakhshari understands them more generally as writings plainly visible. On recitation, Nafi' and Ya'qub read the verb in the second person, "you remember," while the majority read it in the third person, "they remember," a reading Abu 'Ubayd prefers.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the statement that the Qur'an is a sufficient reminder: whoever wills may remember, and the pronoun refers either to the Qur'an or to the reminder. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baqa'i and Ibn 'Ashur understand the human will here as real and as the basis of responsibility. Most, such as Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi, link the following phrase, that they will not remember unless God wills, to the dependence of every action on the divine will. Al-Zamakhshari reads it as God compelling them to remember, but al-Razi rejects this, arguing that an absolute will necessarily produces remembrance and should not be restricted to coercion. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di stress that nothing happens outside God's will, and the latter sees in this a refutation of those who deny human will or deny any real human action. On the closing phrase, the commentators agree that God is worthy of being feared and worthy of forgiving. They cite the hadith of Anas that God has the right to be feared and not associated with, and that He forgives whoever fears Him in this way; Ibn Kathir considers its chain weak while al-Tirmidhi calls it good. Al-Tabari and Qatada explain that God deserves that His prohibitions be respected and that He forgives the sins of the one who repents. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi add that forgiveness follows faith and obedience, while al-Qurtubi reports two views on whether the forgiveness covers major and minor sins alike.

This verse closes the surah's warning to the Quraysh who turn away from the Qur'an. Its plain sense is that the Qur'an is a reminder, and whoever wills may take heed, yet they will not remember unless God wills it. Al-Tabari explains that no one can do anything except that God wills it and grants the ability to do it. Al-Qurtubi reads it the same way: they cannot be admonished without God's will. Ibn Kathir compares the phrase to the verse of Surah 76, verse 30.

The commentators agree that the verse affirms that divine will governs human acts, and that God deserves both piety and forgiveness. Al-Sa'di sees in it a reply to two opposing views: the Qadariyya, who deny that human actions fall under God's will, and the Jabariyya, who deny that humans have any real will. He affirms a genuine human will that follows the divine will.

The main disagreement concerns the meaning of will in the exception. Al-Zamakhshari reads it as compulsion: God would force them to remember, since their hearts are sealed and they would never believe by choice. Al-Razi reports this Mu'tazili reading and rejects it, arguing that the exception refers to absolute will, so remembrance happens whenever God wills it. Muqatil understands it as God granting them guidance.

As for the closing phrase, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to mean that God deserves to be feared, so his prohibitions should be avoided, and that he forgives those who repent. Ibn Ashur reads it as an exclusive statement: God alone deserves to be feared. A report from Anas explains the verse in the same sense, but Ibn Kathir considers its chain weak, and al-Tirmidhi calls it hasan gharib.
